**Audience**: a product / data engineer who ships A/B tests and wants an honest pipeline. **Empirical first**: a "significant" p-value after peeking; underpowered design → business false negative — then we name experimental design, randomization, bootstrap, multiplicity.

The statistician's craft on real data: a differentiator in an AI master's.

### What you will be able to do

-   Run the complete cycle of a statistical study, from the initial question to communicable conclusions.
-   Design an experimental plan: randomization, blocks, and a power computation suited to the objective.
-   Identify the biases of observational studies and the classic pitfalls of inference.
-   Apply the basics of causal inference: potential outcomes and difference-in-differences (DiD).
-   Practice regression for real: diagnostics, transformations, reasoned decisions.
-   Correct multiple tests (Bonferroni, Benjamini-Hochberg) according to the goal.
-   Build intervals and tests by bootstrap on arbitrary data.
-   Run a modern A/B test: sequential, targeted effects — and report the results honestly.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

According to the [APM_52066_EP — "Statistique en Action"](https://synapses.polytechnique.fr/catalogue/2026-2027/ue/680/APM-52066-EP-statistique-en-action) description: the official objective is to show students how statistics are used in practice to answer a precise question, by introducing a series of important model-based approaches. Students learn to select and use the appropriate strategic methodologies, on concrete examples of real datasets from different fields — medicine, genomics, ecology, among others. All analyses are carried out in R; knowledge of R programming is not required (only basic scripting). The detailed session-by-session syllabus is not published on the description (not communicated); the course unit does however appear in the 2026-2027 catalog via the "P2 – Applied Mathematics" track of the engineering cycle, without appearing in the SynapseS composition of the LLGA track S2.

  Official item (SynapseS)                                   Course section
  ---------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Statistics used in practice to answer a precise question   ch1 — The life cycle of a statistical study, and ch3 — Observational versus experimental
  A series of important model-based approaches               ch4 — Causal inference, ch5 — Regression in practice, ch7 — The bootstrap
  Real data from medicine, genomics, ecology…                ch9 — Case study: agricultural trials and blocks (partial coverage: application fields and the historical line of experimental designs)
  All analyses carried out in R                              not explicitly covered: these materials remain software-independent

*Complement to the official syllabus —* the themes structuring these materials (experimental designs and power computation, multiple testing, sequential A/B testing, honest communication of uncertainties) extend the official description, which remains general; they correspond to the historical topics of the MAP566 course associated with this course unit.

### Where this course fits in the program

Module of period 2 of M1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS), offered as an option: the methodological "reality check" of the master's program, taught by Zacharie Naulet (École Polytechnique & INRAE, MaIAGE team). Official prerequisites: not communicated (the "Prerequisites" tab of the SynapseS description is empty); the description only specifies that no knowledge of R is required, basic scripting being sufficient.

-   **Prerequisites** — the background of [Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html) (tests, intervals, estimation) and the framework of [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html); the review section reactivates the "survival kit" actually used afterwards.
-   **Downstream modules** — the culture of intervals, bootstrap and uncertainty built here directly feeds [Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html) (M2), which deepens the uncertainty quantification of models.

### Course outline

-   **Review: the statistician's survival kit** — the only results from the statistics course that are really used, every week.
-   **The life cycle of a statistical study** — from question to report: the map of the craft.
-   **Experimental designs: randomization, blocks, power** — deciding *before* collecting how many and how.
-   **Observational versus experimental: biases** — why we do not always randomize, and what that costs.
-   **Causal inference: potential outcomes and DiD** — approaching a causal effect with imperfect data.
-   **Regression in practice: diagnostics and transformations** — using, checking and repairing a regression model.
-   **Multiple testing: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg** — what to do when testing many hypotheses at once.
-   **The bootstrap in practice** — intervals without closed formulas, on almost any statistic.
-   **A/B testing: sequential and targeted effects** — the randomized trial as digital platforms practice it.
-   **Case study: agricultural trials and blocks** — the historical origin of experimental designs, on a complete case.
-   **Communicating: intervals, p-values, honest visualizations** — making results readable without distorting them.
-   **Course research notes (Naulet, MaIAGE)** — a tour of the research work of Zacharie Naulet.
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Validate the "survival kit" of the review section: it, and not an advanced chapter, determines your ease throughout the module.
-   Work through each section on a real dataset: this course's specificity is that obstacles come from the data, not from formulas.
-   Simulate: the power of a test, the inflation of false positives under multiple testing and the coverage of the bootstrap are understood in a few lines of code.
-   Before every analysis, write the plan — hypotheses, sample size, criterion: the reflex this module seeks to instill.
-   Apply the same rigor to your machine learning models: evaluating a model is a statistical study in its own right.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; the final case study brings them all together.

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} In a master's program oriented toward LLMs and graphs, this module brings the discipline that makes everything else credible: A/B tests and rigorous evaluation are the daily life of the product teams deploying models, and the culture of uncertainty continues in M2 in [Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html). It is also a sought-after profile in research — at the interface with applied sciences, as at INRAE — and in industrial data science wherever decisions have consequences.
:::

## 0. Review: the statistician's survival kit {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used (cf. Refresher Statistics module)
:::

-   **Convergence and limit theorems** (ch. 4): law of large numbers, CLT $\sqrt{n}(\bar X_n - \mu) \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, delta method and bootstrap — the engine of almost every approximation in this module;
-   **Parametric estimation** (ch. 5): bias, variance, quadratic error, maximum likelihood estimators and their asymptotic properties;
-   **Confidence intervals and tests** (ch. 6): level, power, p-value, type I and II errors, two-sample Student test, chi-square test;
-   **Linear regression** (ch. 7): ordinary least squares, Gauss-Markov, tests on the coefficients, $R^2$ — chapter 5 of this module revisits this foundation "on misbehaving data";
-   **Monte Carlo simulation**: generating laws, checking a method by simulation — the permanent working tool of the applied statistician (and of all the labs in this course).
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Statistical model and data]{.tag} A statistical model for data $x_1, \dots, x_n$ is a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta \in \Theta}$ of candidate laws. In practice, the question is not "is the model true?" (it never is) but rather: *what question are we asking the data, and which quantity $\psi(\theta)$* — mean effect, difference of rates, quantile, coefficient — *answers that question?* The whole module is organized around this triptych: **question → collection plan → estimation + uncertainty**. The formula $\bar x \pm 1.96\, s/\sqrt{n}$ from Refresher Statistics is legitimate only if the collection plan is: this module deals with what happens before and around the formula.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — The bias-variance identity and what it implies]{.tag} For every square-integrable estimator $\hat\theta$ of $\theta$: $$\mathbb{E}\big[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}\hat\theta - \theta\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)}_{\text{variance}}.$$

::: proof
Set $\mu = \mathbb{E}\hat\theta$ and expand $\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta-\mu) + (\mu - \theta)]^2 = \mathbb{E}(\hat\theta-\mu)^2 + 2(\mu-\theta)\underbrace{\mathbb{E}(\hat\theta - \mu)}_{=0} + (\mu-\theta)^2$. The cross term is zero because $\mu$ is the expectation of $\hat\theta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

In practice, the bias mostly comes from the **plan** (selection, confounding) and the variance from the **sample size**: increasing $n$ never corrects a selection bias — this is the central message of chapters 2 and 3.
::::

::: note
[Position in the master's program]{.tag} This module is the "craft" complement of Refresher Statistics: less new theory, more *decisions*. It also prepares the M2 module "Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification", which pushes the uncertainty question as far as the calibration of predictive models; the statistics–ML bridge is provided by the Machine Learning module (ch. 1 and 7), and the processing of textual data by the NLP module.
:::

## 1. The life cycle of a statistical study {#ch1}

Concrete scene: an A/B stopped too early that "proves" a nonexistent lift. This chapter structures the question before the data.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Peeking without correction; forgotten multiple testing; confusing correlation and causation without design.
:::

A real statistical study does not begin with a dataset: it begins with a **question**. The diagram below structures the whole module; each chapter tackles a link where studies typically fail.

  Step                Key question                                     Where it breaks                               Chapter
  ------------------- ------------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------- ---------
  1\. Question        Which effect, on which population, which unit?   Vague question, undefined indicator           ch. 1
  2\. Plan            Can we randomize? Block? How many units?         Underpowered, no randomization                ch. 2
  3\. Collection      Who enters the sample? Who leaves it?            Selection bias, survival bias, missing data   ch. 3
  4\. Analysis        Which estimator? Which diagnostics?              Mis-specified model, multiple tests           ch. 5–6
  5\. Uncertainty     Intervals, bootstrap, robustness                 Underestimated uncertainty                    ch. 7
  6\. Communication   What to report, in what form?                    Over-interpreted p-value, misleading chart    ch. 10

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Population, sample, statistical unit, indicator]{.tag} The **population** is the set of units the question concerns; the **sample** is the observed subset; the **statistical unit** is the grain at which we measure (a patient, a field, a user, a query); the **indicator** (or *outcome*, *OEC* for "Overall Evaluation Criterion" in online experimentation) is the quantity measured. A study is *externally valid* if the sample allows an answer for the target population; *internally valid* if the comparisons made within the sample are reliable. One can be internally valid and externally wrong (a trial on healthy volunteers).
:::

::: note
[Reproducibility: HARKing and the garden of forking paths]{.tag} Two documented pathologies: **HARKing** (Kerr, 1998 — hypotheses formulated *after* seeing the results, presented as *a priori*) and the "garden of forking paths" (Gelman & Loken, 2013): without any fraud, the mere freedom to choose the specification *after the fact* (control variables, coding, exclusion of points, subgroups) multiplies the tests actually performed far beyond those reported. Practical answers: pre-registration of the analysis plan, reproducible scripts, reports of every look taken at the data — exactly the disciplines of ch. 8 for A/B testing.
:::

## 2. Experimental designs: randomization, blocks, power {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Randomized experiment (Fisher, 1935)]{.tag} $n$ experimental units receive $K$ treatments; the assignment is drawn **at random** among the possible allocations (with possible balance constraints). Randomization plays three roles: (i) on average, it balances *all* factors, measured or not; (ii) it grounds an *exact* test of the null effect (prop. 2.2); (iii) it legitimizes the causal inference of ch. 4. Historical note: the "lady tasting tea" experiment (Fisher, 1935) — 8 cups, 4 "milk first", 4 "tea first", randomized order.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Exact randomization test, computed by hand]{.tag} Six plots with yields 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (q/ha; teaching data) receive A or B, three each. Observed: A = {6, 7, 8}, B = {3, 4, 5}, difference of means $\hat d = 7 - 4 = 3$. Under the null hypothesis "no effect", $\hat d$ takes each of the $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ values $\bar x_A - \bar x_B$ with probability $1/20$. The largest possible value of $\|\hat d\|$ is 3, reached only for the splits {6,7,8} and {3,4,5} (the split {5,7,8} against {3,4,6} gives $\hat d = 6.67 - 4.33 = 2.33 \< 3$). Therefore $$p \;=\; \mathbb{P}\big(\|\hat d\| \geq 3 \,\big\|\, H_0\big) \;=\; \frac{2}{20} \;=\; 0.10 \quad\text{(exact, without any distributional assumption).}$$

::: proof
The only thing used: under $H_0$, the treatment does not influence the yield, so the observed value of $\hat d$ is piecewise constant and only the assignment is random; the assignment being uniform over the 20 balanced allocations, the p-value is the proportion of allocations at least as extreme. Enumerating the 20 splits (or a symmetry argument on A/B) gives exactly 2 splits with $\|\bar x_A - \bar x_B\| = 3$ and all others $\leq 2.33$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Randomized complete block design (RCBD)]{.tag} When the units are heterogeneous but can be grouped into homogeneous **blocks** (neighboring plots, production days, hospitals), one draws *independently within each block* a permutation of the $K$ treatments. Analysis model: $$y_{ij} = \mu + \tau_i + \beta_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \ \text{i.i.d.},$$ with $\tau_i$ the effect of treatment $i$, $\beta_j$ the effect of block $j$. Blocks turn the variability *between* units into an explicit factor: ch. 9 shows, on numerical data, a variance gain by a factor of 30 and more.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Sample size for a target power (two-sample Gaussian test)]{.tag} To test $H_0 : \mu_A = \mu_B$ against $\mu_B - \mu_A = \delta$ at level $\alpha$ (two-sided) with common variance $\sigma^2$, $n$ measurements per group and the normal approximation, the power is $$\pi(\delta) \;=\; \Phi\!\Big( \frac{\delta}{\sigma}\sqrt{\tfrac{n}{2}} - z_{1-\alpha/2} \Big),$$ and power $1 - \beta$ is reached for $$n \;=\; \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{(\delta/\sigma)^2} \quad \text{measurements per group.}$$

::: proof
The test rejects when $\|\hat d\| \> z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$ with $\hat d = \bar y_B - \bar y_A \sim \mathcal{N}(\delta, 2\sigma^2/n)$. Under the alternative, $\mathbb{P}(\hat d \< -s) \approx 0$ (with $s = z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$ and $\delta \> 0$), so $\pi = \mathbb{P}(\hat d \> s) = \Phi\big(\tfrac{\delta - s}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}\big) = \Phi\big(\tfrac{\delta}{\sigma}\sqrt{\tfrac n2} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\big)$. Writing $\pi = 1 - \beta$ amounts to $\tfrac{\delta}{\sigma}\sqrt{\tfrac n2} - z_{1-\alpha/2} = z_{1-\beta}$, hence the formula by isolating $n$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Power computed, and a sizing table]{.tag} We want to detect $\delta = 0.3\,\sigma$ (a *small* but economically relevant effect) with $\alpha = 5\,\%$ and 80 % power: $z_{0.975} = 1.960$, $z_{0.8} = 0.842$, $$n = \frac{2\,(1.960 + 0.842)^2}{0.3^2} = \frac{2 \times 7.85}{0.09} = 174.4 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{175 \text{ units per group}}.$$ Complete table (values rounded up):

  $\delta/\sigma$   Power 80 %   Power 90 %   Reading
  ------------------- ------------ ------------ --------------------------------
  0.2                 393          526          very small effect: costly
  0.3                 175          234          our case
  0.5                 63           85           medium effect
  0.8                 25           33           large effect: a pilot suffices

Professional moral: **half the power is paid in the square root of n, doubling the precision costs ×4 the sample**, and nobody "finds" an effect of 0.2σ with 30 observations. In practice one replaces $\sigma^2$ with an estimate from a pilot or the literature, and $\delta$ with the smallest *useful* effect (the minimum clinically or economically relevant difference), never with the effect one hopes for.
:::

::: note
[Power a priori, never a posteriori]{.tag} Power is a *design* tool. The "observed power" computed after the fact with $\hat\delta$ is a monotone transformation of the p-value: it brings no new information and muddles the report (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). What should be reported: the confidence interval of the effect (ch. 10).
:::

## 3. Observational versus experimental: biases {#ch3}

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Observational study, confounding factor]{.tag} A study is **observational** when the assignment of "treatments" (exposure, product, degree) is not controlled by the experimenter. A **confounding factor** $Z$ is a variable that influences both the exposure and the response; it creates a "natural" difference of means between groups even without any effect. Canonical example: ice cream sales and drownings (confounded by weather). Adjustment (standardization, regression, matching) only corrects *measured* confounders; randomization also neutralizes the unmeasured ones — that is the whole difference between ch. 2 and the present chapter.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Simpson's paradox, real data: kidney stones (Charig et al., 1986)]{.tag} Historical comparison of two kidney stone treatments (B: minimally invasive surgery; A: open surgery), % success:

  Stratum        Treatment A          Treatment B
  -------------- -------------------- --------------------
  Small stones   **81/87 = 93 %**     234/270 = 87 %
  Large stones   **192/263 = 73 %**   55/80 = 69 %
  **Overall**    273/350 = 78 %       **289/350 = 83 %**

A is better in *every* stratum and worse *in aggregate*: B was preferentially given to small stones (easy cases). This is a pure confounding effect by severity, mechanically reversible by standardization.

::: proof
Let $p_{ks}$ be the success rate of treatment $k$ in stratum $s$ and $w_s^{(k)}$ the proportion of patients of stratum $s$ in group $k$. The overall rate of group $k$ is $\sum_s w_s^{(k)}\, p_{ks}$: it mixes effectiveness ($p$) and case mix ($w$). B can win in aggregate with $p_{Bs} \leq p_{As}$ for every $s$ as soon as $w^{(B)}$ loads the easy strata: here $w^{(B)}_{\text{small}} = 270/350 = 0.77$ versus $87/350 = 0.25$ for A. Standardizing on a common profile $w$ (e.g. $w^{(A)}$) restores A's advantage in each stratum, hence on average. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Selection bias and survivorship bias]{.tag} **Selection bias**: the sample is not representative of the target population (volunteers, trade shows, survey respondents). **Survivorship bias**: the special case where the filter is *survival / still being in activity*; the departed carry their bad results away with them.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Two worked examples]{.tag} **(a) Wald's airplanes (1943).** Returning from missions, bullet holes concentrate on the wings and fuselage, almost none on the engines. Reinforcing the hit zones would be the survivor's error: planes hit in the engine *do not come back*. The armor goes where the survivors are *untouched*. (The episode, popularized by W. Allen, is reconstructed and discussed by Mangel & Samuels, 2002.)\
\
**(b) Mutual funds (teaching figures calibrated on Elton, Gruber & Blake, 1996).** Of 200 funds existing in 2015, 100 closed before 2025. Advertising cites the average return of the 100 survivors: 8 %/year. The 100 vanished ones made −5 %/year before closing. The return actually experienced by a 2015 investor: $$\frac{100 \times 8 + 100 \times (-5)}{200} = 1.5\,\%/\text{year} \quad \text{versus} \quad 8\,\% \text{ displayed.}$$ Over 10 years, a compounded gap of 1 %/year ≈ 10 % of missing final wealth — enough to rank every product on the market differently.
:::

::: note
[Where do you meet these biases in ML?]{.tag} Everywhere: models trained on *current* customers (churners do not notify their departure); evaluations of a recruitment system on hires (non-hires have no observed performance — this is the crux of ch. 4); academic benchmarks filtered by the publications that use them (failures are not submitted). Reflex: always ask *how the sample was constituted and who dropped out of it*.
:::

## 4. Causal inference: potential outcomes and DiD {#ch4}

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Potential outcomes, ATE (Neyman 1923; Rubin 1974)]{.tag} For each unit $i$ and treatment $w \in \{0, 1\}$, we posit two *potential* outcomes $Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$; the individual effect is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ and the **average effect** $\mathrm{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[\tau_i]$. We only ever observe one value $Y_i = W_i Y_i(1) + (1 - W_i) Y_i(0)$: the fundamental causal problem is a **missing data** problem (cf. Refresher Statistics, ch. 9). Two *a priori* assumptions: *consistency* (the observed value equals the potential outcome of the received treatment) and *no interference* (the treatment of unit $j$ does not affect $i$) — together [SUTVA]{style="white-space:nowrap"}.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Randomization debiases the difference of means]{.tag} If $W \perp (Y(0), Y(1))$ (unbiased randomization), then $\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$ is unbiased for the ATE, and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau) \approx \frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_0^2}{n_0}$.

::: proof
$\mathbb{E}[\bar Y_1 \mid W] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) \mid W = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$ by independence, and likewise for $\bar Y_0$, hence $\mathbb{E}\hat\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)] = \mathrm{ATE}$. The two means are over disjoint, hence independent, groups, which gives the sum of the empirical variances. [∎]{.qed}
:::

In an observational setting, $W$ is *self-selected*: $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\mid W{=}1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid W{=}0]$ mixes the causal effect with selection. The whole modern machinery (adjustment, matching, instrumental variables, DiD) aims at reconstructing a randomized comparison.
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Difference-in-differences, the sketch]{.tag} Two groups (treated, control), two dates (before, after), without randomization: $$\widehat{\mathrm{DiD}} \;=\; \big(\bar Y_{\text{after, treated}} - \bar Y_{\text{before, treated}}\big) - \big(\bar Y_{\text{after, control}} - \bar Y_{\text{before, control}}\big).$$ Central assumption: **parallel trends** — without treatment, the treated/control gap would have stayed constant; the control serves as a "trajectory counterfactual". This is the most used causal identification in applied economics since Card & Krueger (1994).
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — Minimum wage New Jersey / Pennsylvania (Card & Krueger, 1994)]{.tag} Rise of the NJ minimum wage (April 1992); neighboring Pennsylvania serves as the control. Average full-time employment (FTE) per restaurant:

                           Before   After   Change
  ------------------------ -------- ------- --------
  New Jersey (treated)     20.44    21.03   +0.59
  Pennsylvania (control)   23.33    21.17   −2.16

$$\widehat{\mathrm{DiD}} = 0.59 - (-2.16) = +2.75 \ \text{FTE} \quad (\approx +11\,\% \text{ vs before}).$$ The regional economy was depressing both states; the naive "NJ before/after" comparison (+0.59) would underestimate the effect, and the "NJ/PA after" comparison (−1.14 FTE) would outright flip its sign: only the double difference neutralizes the common shock. Crucial methodological point (Bertrand, Duflo & Mullainathan, 2004): naive DiD standard errors are massively too small because of serial correlation — one must cluster by unit or aggregate.
:::

::: note
[Further]{.tag} Causal graphs and the back-door criterion (Pearl), instrumental variables, regression discontinuity: beyond the sketch of this module — see Imbens & Rubin (2015). The link with ML (estimating effect heterogeneity with causal forests) is covered in the Machine Learning module, and the Graph ML module for the dependence structure.
:::

## 5. Regression in practice: diagnostics and transformations {#ch5}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminders (cf. Refresher Statistics module, ch. 7)
:::

-   OLS estimator $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$, residuals $e = y - \hat y$, hat matrix $H = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$, $\hat y = Hy$;
-   Gauss-Markov: BLUE under i.i.d. zero-mean errors; Student tests if moreover Gaussian;
-   The Machine Learning module (ch. 2) covers ridge/lasso regularization — here we stay in inferential mode: the coefficients *are* the object of interest.
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Leverage and Cook's distance]{.tag} The leverage of observation $i$ is $h_{ii}$, the diagonal of $H$; $\sum_i h_{ii} = p$ (number of parameters), $0 \leq h_{ii} \leq 1$. Cook's distance $$D_i = \frac{e_i^2}{p\,s^2}\cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}$$ measures the influence of $i$ on the whole set of coefficients. Leverage point: $h_{ii} \> 2p/n$; influential point: $D_i \> 4/n$.

::: proof
For the trace: $H$ is an orthogonal projector (onto im $X$), and the trace of a projector equals its rank $= \mathrm{rank}(X) = p$. Removing row $i$ and re-estimating gives $\hat\beta - \hat\beta_{(-i)} = \frac{(X^\top X)^{-1}x_i e_i}{1 - h_{ii}}$; Cook's distance standardizes this variation by the dispersion $p s^2$ of the estimators — hence the formula: the residual alone (an outlier can be well predicted!) or the leverage alone (an extreme point can be perfectly aligned) do not suffice; it is their *product* that tips the line. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — The four diagnostic plots]{.tag} **(1) Residuals vs fitted values**: curvature ⇒ non-linearity (add quadratic terms, splines); funnel ⇒ heteroscedasticity. **(2) Q-Q of residuals**: heavy tails ⇒ fragile intervals/Student tests at small $n$. **(3) Scale-location** ($\sqrt{\|e\|}$ vs $\hat y$): checks the constancy of $s^2$. **(4) Residuals vs leverage (Cook)**: hunts influential points. Professional reflex: these four plots *before* any interpretation, systematically.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Transformations: the log as a universal tool]{.tag} Prices of 30 goods ($y$, euros) against surface area ($x$, m²). Typical symptoms: funnel-shaped residuals, the line pulled by a few very high-leverage luxury goods. **Remedy**: regress $\log y$ on $\log x$: $$\log y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log x_i + \varepsilon_i \iff y_i = e^{\beta_0}\, x_i^{\beta_1}\, e^{\varepsilon_i}.$$ $\beta_1$ becomes an **elasticity**: $+1\,\%$ of surface ⇒ $+\beta_1\,\%$ of price. If $\hat\beta_1 = 1.08$, the interpretation "each extra square meter adds 8 %" replaces the fragile linear interpretation "each square meter adds €3,120" — wrong for a studio as for a mansion. The log transformation: (i) symmetrizes distributions and stabilizes variance when the effect is multiplicative; (ii) crushes extreme leverages; (iii) makes errors *relative*, which is often the right physical/economic model. General family: Box-Cox $y^{(\lambda)} = (y^\lambda - 1)/\lambda$, with $\lambda$ chosen by profile likelihood; special cases $\lambda = 1$ (identity), $\lambda = 0$ (log), $\lambda = 1/2$ (square root, Poisson).
:::

::: note
[Heteroscedasticity: robust errors, no panic]{.tag} Heteroscedasticity does *not* bias $\hat\beta$ (Gauss-Markov only needs homoscedasticity for efficiency, not consistency); it distorts the standard errors. Modern solution: sandwich estimators (White, HC1) — $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathrm{diag}(e_i^2) X (X^\top X)^{-1}$ — available everywhere (`statsmodels`, `sandwich` in R). With grouped or panel data, cluster by unit (cf. ch. 4, Bertrand et al. 2004).
:::

## 6. Multiple testing: Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg {#ch6}

The modern statistician tests thousands of hypotheses at once (genomics, multi-metric A/B testing, subgroup analyses). Testing $m$ true null hypotheses each at $\alpha = 5\,\%$ produces on average $\alpha m$ false positives — with $m = 1000$: 50 "discoveries" in pure noise. One must choose what to control.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — FWER and FDR]{.tag} Among $R$ rejected hypotheses of which $V$ are false (false positives): $$\mathrm{FWER} = \mathbb{P}(V \geq 1) \qquad \text{(at least one error)}$$ $$\mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \frac{V}{R \vee 1} \right] \qquad \text{(expected proportion of errors).}$$ Controlling the FWER is required when a single false discovery is costly (pivotal clinical trial); controlling the FDR is enough for exploration (differential expression, product optimization) — we accept some noise among the discoveries.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Bonferroni controls the FWER]{.tag} Rejecting the $p_i \leq \alpha/m$ gives $\mathrm{FWER} \leq \alpha$.

::: proof
Union bound (Boole): if an error is made, at least one p-value under a true null has crossed its threshold, so $$\mathrm{FWER} \leq \mathbb{P}\Big( \bigcup_{i \in I_0} \{p_i \leq \alpha/m\} \Big) \leq \sum_{i \in I_0} \frac{\alpha}{m} \leq \frac{m_0\,\alpha}{m} \leq \alpha,$$ where $m_0 \leq m$ is the number of true nulls. No independence is required. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Price to pay: as $m$ grows, the threshold $\alpha/m$ becomes untenable ($m = 10^4$ ⇒ $5 \times 10^{-6}$) and power collapses; the Šidák variant ($1 - (1-\alpha)^{1/m}$, exact under independence) does not change the order of magnitude.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Benjamini-Hochberg controls the FDR (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)]{.tag} Let $p_{(1)} \leq \dots \leq p_{(m)}$ be the sorted p-values and $$k^\* = \max\Big\{ k : p_{(k)} \leq \frac{k}{m}\,q \Big\}.$$ Rejecting the $k^\*$ smallest p-values (none if the set is empty) controls $\mathrm{FDR} \leq \frac{m_0}{m} q \leq q$ when the p-values under true nulls are independent of each other and of the rest (extension: PRDS positive dependence, Benjamini & Yekutieli 2001; otherwise, replace $q$ by $q / \sum_{k=1}^m 1/k$).

::: proof
**Case where all nulls are true ($m_0 = m$).** Then $V = R$ whenever $R \geq 1$, so $V/(R \vee 1) = \mathbf{1}\{R \geq 1\}$ and $\mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{P}(R \geq 1)$. Now $R \geq 1$ requires $p_{(1)} \leq q/m$, and $p_{(1)} = \min_i p_i$ with i.i.d. uniform $p_i$: $$\mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{P}\Big(\min_i p_i \leq \frac{q}{m}\Big) = 1 - \Big(1 - \frac{q}{m}\Big)^m \;\leq\; q.$$ **General case (sketch).** Decompose $\mathrm{FDR} = \sum_{i \in I_0} \mathbb{E}\big[ \tfrac{1}{R} \mathbf{1}\{p_i \leq p_{(k^\*)}\}\big]$ over the rejection rank. The two ingredients of the complete proof (Benjamini & Hochberg, Thm 1): (i) for each null $i$, the event "$i$ rejected at rank $r$" requires $p_i \leq qr/m$ *and* at least $r - 1$ of the other p-values $\leq qr/m$; (ii) by independence of $p_i$ from the rest, the product of probabilities yields a factor $qr/m$, which, killed by the $1/r$ of the weighting, leaves the bound $\frac{q}{m}$ — then the telescoping summation over ranks (Abel's transformation) bounds the total by $\frac{m_0}{m} q$. The subtlety (and beauty) of the result: the *data-dependent* threshold $q k^\*/m$ "self-adjusts" to the number of apparent discoveries. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — BH computed, against Bonferroni]{.tag} $m = 10$ p-values: 0.001 · 0.004 · 0.009 · 0.019 · 0.021 · 0.031 · 0.043 · 0.71 · 0.88 · 0.92. With $q = 0.05$:

  $k$   $p_{(k)}$   threshold $qk/m$   BH decision
  ----- ------------ ------------------ ----------------------
  1     0.001        0.005              reject
  2     0.004        0.010              reject
  3     0.009        0.015              reject
  4     0.019        0.020              reject
  5     **0.021**    **0.025**          **reject (k\* = 5)**
  6     0.031        0.030              stop

BH rejects $k^\* = 5$ hypotheses (all p ≤ 0.021); Bonferroni at $\alpha = 0.05$ rejects only $p \leq 0.005$: 2 hypotheses. If the first 5 nulls are false, Bonferroni leaves 3 discoveries on the table; BH in exchange claims $\leq 5\,\%$ false positives *in proportion*. In the lab, we will verify by simulation (exercise 5) that the empirical FDR of BH settles at $q\, m_0/m$.
:::

::: note
[Adaptive and genomic version]{.tag} If many nulls are false, $m_0/m$ makes BH conservative. Adaptive procedures estimate $\pi_0 = m_0/m$ (Storey, 2002 — the large p-values are almost all true nulls) and gain power. This is the default setting of differential analyses in genomics (`qvalue`, `IHW`). Internal link: estimating $\pi_0$ and the "missing mass" is exactly a species sampling problem — a research axis of the instructor (ch. 11).
:::

## 7. The bootstrap in practice {#ch7}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder (cf. Refresher Statistics module, ch. 4)
:::

The nonparametric bootstrap resamples $B$ times, *with replacement*, $n$ observations, recomputes the statistic on each resample, and reads the variability off the bootstrap distribution. Here we push through to intervals, edge cases and code.
::::

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — The plug-in principle (Efron, 1979)]{.tag} The empirical law $\hat P_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \delta_{x_i}$ is the natural nonparametric estimator of the unknown law $P$. The bootstrap *simulates* the inference problem by replacing $P$ with $\hat P_n$: if $T_n = t(x_1, \dots, x_n\,; P)$ is the statistic of interest, its bootstrap version $T_n^\* = t(x_1^\*, \dots, x_n^\* ; \hat P_n)$ is computed by Monte Carlo. Ideal: the law of $T_n^\* - t(\hat P_n)$ approximates that of $T_n - t(P)$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — Consistency for the mean (and beyond, sketch)]{.tag} If $x_i$ are i.i.d., $\mathbb{E}X^2 \< \infty$, the law of $\sqrt n(\bar x^\* - \bar x)$ conditional on the data converges to the same limit $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ as $\sqrt n(\bar x_n - \mu)$.

::: proof
Conditional on the data, the $x_i^\*$ are i.i.d. with law $\hat P_n$, expectation $\bar x$ and variance $\hat\sigma_n^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$. The CLT applied to this sequence (for almost every draw of the data) gives $\sqrt n(\bar x^\* - \bar x) \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0, \hat\sigma_n^2)$, and $\hat\sigma_n^2 \to \sigma^2$ almost surely (LLN) — the conditional Slutsky lemma concludes. The same scheme holds for *regular* functionals of $P$ (differentiable functionals — functional delta method); this is the subject of the empirical Donsker theorem and van der Vaart's theory (ch. 23). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 7.3 — Three intervals for the median]{.tag} Eight response times (ms): 118, 132, 127, 141, 122, 135, 128, 240 (one heavy point). Observed median: $(128+132)/2 = 130$. A "hand-made" normal CI: delicate (no simple $\sqrt n$ formula for the median). Bootstrap with $B = 2000$: draw 2000 resamples, each yields a median $m_b^\*$; take the 2.5 % and 97.5 % percentiles; typical output: CI ≈ \[124; 137\]. The *basic* interval (reverse percentile) reverses: $[2\hat m - q_{97.5}^\*,\ 2\hat m - q_{2.5}^\*]$, which corrects a version bias; BCa additionally readjusts for bias and skewness via jackknife. Reading rule: if percentile and basic differ strongly, the bootstrap distribution is very asymmetric — a signal in itself.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

x = np.array([118, 132, 127, 141, 122, 135, 128, 240])
n, B = len(x), 5000
med_star = np.median(rng.choice(x, size=(B, n), replace=True), axis=1)
mhat = np.median(x)

# 1. percentile: quantiles of the bootstrap law
lo, hi = np.quantile(med_star, [0.025, 0.975])
# 2. basic (reverse percentile): symmetrization around the estimate
lo_b, hi_b = 2*mhat - hi, 2*mhat - lo
print(f"mediane = {mhat}, IC percentile [{lo:.0f}, {hi:.0f}], IC basic [{lo_b:.0f}, {hi_b:.0f}]")
# 3. bootstrap bias: E*[m*] - mhat
print(f"biais bootstrap estime : {med_star.mean() - mhat:+.2f} ms")
```

::: note
[When the bootstrap fails]{.tag} **Dependent data**: the i.i.d. bootstrap breaks the structure — use the block bootstrap (weather, financial series, web streams); **extremes and deep quantiles**: the empirical law does not have a rich enough tail; **small $n$** (\< 10): the empirical law is too coarse a scale (at most $n^n$ distinct resamples, and often far fewer distinct values of the statistic); **non-regular statistics** (boundaries, number of components): the bootstrap can be inconsistent. Research bridge: Naulet, Roy, Sharma & Veitch use *weighted* bootstraps for the graphex tail index — the estimator of the "hidden mass" of large networks (ch. 11).
:::

## 8. A/B testing: sequential and targeted effects {#ch8}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — A/B test and OEC]{.tag} An online randomized experiment: every unit (user, query, session — *the randomization unit must be the analysis unit*) receives variant A (control) or B (treatment). The **OEC** (Overall Evaluation Criterion) is the single decision metric, defined *before* the experiment; secondary metrics (guardrails: latency, error rate, churn) are tested with multiple-testing correction (ch. 6). Discipline: no OEC, no test.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.2 — The cost of "peeking" (looking before the end)]{.tag} A fixed-horizon test of level $\alpha$, examined $K$ times with stopping as soon as a p-value drops below $\alpha$, has a false positive rate $$\mathbb{P}(\exists k \leq K : p_k \leq \alpha) \;\geq\; \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad \leq\; 1 - (1 - \alpha)^K \ \text{(if independent).}$$ For $K = 5$ looks and $\alpha = 5\,\%$, already $1 - 0.95^5 = 22.6\,\%$; with daily continuous monitoring over weeks, Johari, Pekelis, Walsh and Ye (KDD 2017) measure rates reaching about **three times** the nominal level.

::: proof
The lower bound is clear (the first look is a level-$\alpha$ test). The upper bound: union bound over the $K$ events $\{p_k \leq \alpha\}$, each of probability $\leq \alpha$ under $H_0$ — with equality × independence when the looks are independent tests (a rough approximation: in practice successive p-values are highly correlated, which makes the true rate smaller than the bound but far above $\alpha$). Hence the simulation of exercise 7. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 8.3 — Always-valid p-values and mSPRT (Johari et al., 2017)]{.tag} A sequential p-value $p_t$ is **always valid** if $\mathbb{P}(\exists t : p_t \leq \alpha) \leq \alpha$ for every stopping time — one may then look as often as desired. Construction: a mixture of sequential probability ratio tests (mSPRT); the mirror Bayesian version: monitor the posterior of $d = p_B - p_A$ and its credible interval at every instant (code below), with a non-informative Beta prior; the two families correspond asymptotically (same boundaries in $t$, cf. the Reinforcement Learning module ch. 6 for bandits, the other answer to the problem).
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(52)

# ---- Bayesian A/B test: Beta posteriors, decision by expected loss ----
conv = np.array([1274, 1378])          # conversions
n    = np.array([12000, 12000])        # visits
a, b = 1.0, 1.0                        # Beta(1, 1) prior
post = [rng.beta(conv[i] + a, n[i] - conv[i] + b, size=200_000) for i in range(2)]

d = post[1] - post[0]                  # absolute uplift drawn a posteriori
loss_if_B = np.where(d < 0, -d, 0.0)   # loss if we deploy B and A was better

print(f"P(B > A)            : {(d > 0).mean():.3f}")
print(f"gain median         : {np.median(d):.5f}")
print(f"IC 95 % du gain     : {np.quantile(d, [0.025, 0.975])}")
print(f"E[perte | deploi B] : {loss_if_B.mean():.2e}")
# Typical outputs: P(B>A) = 0.984; median uplift = 0.0087;
# CI = [0.0007, 0.0166]; E[loss] = 2.2e-05.
# Decision: the cost of a wrong choice of B (2 conversions out of 10^5) is negligible
# compared with the expected gain (+0.87 point) -- we deploy B.
```

::: def
[Definition 8.4 — Targeted (heterogeneous) effects and the associated errors]{.tag} The average effect hides heterogeneity: B wins on mobile, loses on desktop. Two symmetric pitfalls: (i) **subgroup spinning**: 20 segments ⇒ expect a "significant gain" in one of them by pure noise (ch. 6, Bonferroni/BH mandatory); (ii) **ignored real interaction effects**: the aggregated OEC can cancel out opposite effects (Simpson, ch. 3). A sound framework: specify segments a priori, test the segment × treatment *interaction*, correct for multiple testing. On the variance side: CUPED (Deng et al., 2013) reuses the metric measured before the experiment as a covariate — a typical "free" variance reduction of 30–50 %, statistically equivalent to the blocks of ch. 2.
:::

::: note
[Interference and validity]{.tag} Two-sided market (Uber: more drivers ⇒ wait time drops for everyone, including the control), CDN caches, social network effects: SUTVA (ch. 4) violated. Answers: randomize by clusters (cities, IP clusters — power loss via the design effect $1 + (m-1)\rho$), or isolate (switchback). See Kohavi, Tang & Xu (2020) for the complete catalog of production pitfalls; the Reinforcement Learning module (bandits, ch. 6) addresses the "exploit during the experiment" alternative.
:::

## 9. Case study: agricultural trials and blocks {#ch9}

Agricultural experimentation is the cradle of experimental design: Fisher at Rothamsted in the 1920s invented randomization, blocks and analysis of variance precisely because plots are heterogeneous — the same problem as your users or your patients. It is also the daily ground of INRAE, the instructor's institution: multi-year multi-location variety trials, complete blocks and *alpha-lattices* (Patterson & Williams, 1976) to screen hundreds of varieties.

::: ex
[Example 9.1 — RCBD computed end to end (teaching data)]{.tag} 4 varieties (A–D) × 5 blocks, yields (t/ha) constructed as $y_{ij} = 50 + \tau_i + \beta_j + e_{ij}$ with variety effects $(+3, +1, -2, -2)$, block effects $(+8, +2, 0, -4, -6)$ and residuals summing to zero row-wise and column-wise:

  Variety   Block 1   Block 2   Block 3   Block 4   Block 5   Mean
  --------- --------- --------- --------- --------- --------- ----------
  A         62        54        53        50        46        **53.0**
  B         60        56        51        48        48        **52.6**
  C         56        54        47        44        42        **48.6**
  D         56        52        49        44        42        **48.6**
  Mean      58.5      54        50        46.5      44.5      50.7

(Values rounded; the sums below use the exact figures of the model.) **Analysis of variance**:

  Source      df   Sum of squares          Mean square   F
  ----------- ---- ----------------------- ------------- ----------
  Varieties   3    SS_v = 5 Σ(τ̂ᵢ)² = 90    30.0          **30.0**
  Blocks      4    SS_b = 4 Σ(β̂ⱼ)² = 480   120.0         120.0
  Residuals   12   SS_e = Σ e² = 12        **1.0**       —

Observed $F_{3,12}$ $= 30$ against a threshold of $F_{0.95;\,3,12} = 3.49$ — highly significant varietal differences. Pairwise comparisons: standard deviation of a difference of means $\sqrt{2 \times 1.0/5} = 0.63$, LSD at the 5 % level: $2.179 \times 0.63 = 1.38$ — A (53.0) \> B (52.6) \> C = D (48.6); A against B is *not* separated (0.4 \< 1.38). **The gain from blocking:** without blocks, the block variability would join the residual: $(480 + 12)/16 = 30.75$ instead of $1.0$ — the same trial under a completely randomized design would have an $F$ on the order of 1: **the trial would have seen nothing**. This is literally Fisher's lesson: planning well beats modeling well after the fact.
:::

::: note
[Natural continuation]{.tag} Multi-environment trials: genotype × environment interactions, AMMI/GGE models (the PCA of the Machine Learning module ch. 6 applied to interactions); resolvable incomplete blocks (alpha-lattices) when $K \>$ block size; spatial analysis (fertility trend by rows/columns). The INRAE thread: dozens of trials, thousands of plots, one imperative — randomize, block, estimate the uncertainty, communicate honestly (ch. 10).
:::

## 10. Communicating: intervals, p-values, honest visualizations {#ch10}

::: thm
[Milestone 10.1 — The ASA's six principles on the p-value (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016)]{.tag}

1.  a p-value measures the incompatibility of the data with a specified statistical model;
2.  it is *not* the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor that the result is due to chance;
3.  scientific conclusions and decisions should not pass only through a threshold (p \< 0.05);
4.  full transparency: correct p-values only with the procedure and analysis reported in full;
5.  a p-value, or statistical significance, measures neither the size of an effect nor its importance;
6.  an isolated p-value proves nothing by itself — facts, context and replication make the proof.

Collective follow-up: Amrhein, Greenland & McShane (2019), "Scientists rise up against statistical significance" — more than 800 signatories: stop classifying results as "significant" / "not significant".
:::

::: ex
[Example 10.2 — Same data, two stories]{.tag} Trial with $n = 40$ per arm, $\hat d = 3.1$ points, $s = 15$, p = 0.041 (two-sided). **Test story:** "significant effect (p = 0.04)" — suggests clear evidence. **Estimation story:** 95 % CI of $d$: $3.1 \pm 1.96 \times 15\sqrt{2/40} = 3.1 \pm 6.6 = [-3.5; 9.7]$: the data are compatible with a null effect, a negative one, or one triple the estimate. The second story is the right one: same numbers, honest information. Corollary: "p = 0.20" does *not* mean "proven that the effect is null" — the CI might be \[−1; +8\]: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
:::

::: def
[Definition 10.3 — Honest visualizations: the rules of the craft]{.tag} **Axes:** never silently truncated on bar charts (a 2 % difference becomes a mountain); bars for counts start at zero, lines may be truncated if stated. **Error bars:** always say what they carry — SD (dispersion of the data), SE (precision of the mean) or a 95 % CI (inference); by default, show the CI. **Raw data:** overlay individual points (jitter, violin) on the summaries — 8 observations do not deserve a boxplot. **Dual axis:** almost always a lie. **Effect size + uncertainty + n** in every figure/caption; never show a percentage without a count. Synthesis reference: Cumming (2014), "The new statistics".
:::

::: ex
[Example 10.3 — Arithmetic of the reproducibility crisis (Ioannidis, 2005)]{.tag} A field tests 1000 hypotheses, 100 of which are true. Power 80 %, $\alpha = 5\,\%$: true positives $= 80$, false positives $= 0.05 \times 900 = 45$. Among the published discoveries ($125$), the proportion of *real* discoveries is $$\frac{80}{80 + 45} = 64\,\%.$$ Lower the power to 20 % (underpowered studies, cf. ch. 2): true positives 20, false 45 ⇒ 31 %. Add the biases of ch. 1 (analytical flexibility, selective publication): the PPV can plummet toward 0 — hence systematic replication, pre-registration, and the "announced n and analysis plan" standards of the industrial A/B testing world.
:::

## 11. Course research notes (Naulet, MaIAGE) {#ch11}

**Zacharie Naulet** is a junior professor (INRAE, MaIAGE team — Mathematics and Computer Science applied to Food and the Environment) and teaches at École Polytechnique; his PhD (Université Paris-Saclay) was on nonparametric Bayesian methods for signal and image processing. His themes — **nonparametric Bayesian statistics, exchangeability, hidden state space models, applications to biological data and networks** — directly feed several chapters of this module: the bootstrap (ch. 7), multiple testing and the estimation of $\pi_0$ (ch. 6), network models (ch. 8–9).

::: ex
[Example 11.1 — Exchangeability and de Finetti: the backbone]{.tag} De Finetti's theorem (1931) states that an infinite sequence of *exchangeable* variables is conditionally i.i.d. with respect to a random law: this is the foundation of Bayesian inference. The quantitative question — how fast does exchangeability approach i.i.d.? — was solved by Dolera & Favaro ("De Finetti's theorem: rate of convergence in Kolmogorov distance", Bernoulli 2020; [arXiv:1802.02244](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.02244)) — work by colleagues in the field, cited here as a standard, *and not* by the instructor. Z. Naulet's work extends the de Finetti program on two fronts:

-   **exchangeable relational data**: V. Veitch, E. Sharma, [Z. Naulet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02311), D. Roy, "Exchangeable modelling of relational data…" — train/test splitting and sparse Poisson factorization for graphs (a bridge with the Graph ML module); Z. Naulet, J. Rousseau, F. Caron, ["Asymptotic Analysis of Statistical Estimators related to MultiGraphex Processes under Misspecification"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01120) — what becomes of the estimators when the graphex model is wrong, a statistician-in-action question;
-   **species sampling**: C. Balocchi, S. Favaro, [Z. Naulet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.06076), "Bayesian Nonparametric Inference for 'Species-sampling' Problems" (Statistical Science): how many species — genetic variants, words, users — have we *not* seen? This is the "missing mass" that also controls the adaptive FDR of ch. 6 (with S. Favaro: ["Optimal estimation of high-order missing masses…"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14998), IEEE Trans. IT; ["Near-optimal estimation of the unseen under regularly varying tail populations"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03251), Bernoulli 2023).
:::

::: ex
[Example 11.2 — From the bootstrap to networks, and the bridge to privacy]{.tag}

-   **Bootstrap for graphs:** Z. Naulet, D. Roy, E. Sharma, V. Veitch, ["Bootstrap estimators for the tail-index and for the count statistics of graphex processes"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.01745) — resampling networks to estimate uncertainty (ch. 7, research version);
-   **hidden models:** K. Abraham, E. Gassiat, [Z. Naulet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16293), "Frontiers to the learning of nonparametric hidden Markov models"; E. Gassiat, I. Kaddouri, [Z. Naulet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12238), "Clustering risk in Non-parametric Hidden Markov and I.I.D. Models"; quantum homodyne tomography with E. Barat ([arXiv:1610.01895](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.01895));
-   **disclosure risk:** F. Camerlenghi, S. Favaro, [Z. Naulet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.05354), F. Panero, "Optimal disclosure risk assessment" (Annals of Statistics, 2021): how far can data be published without re-identifying individuals? — the gateway to the M2 module "Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification";
-   **nonparametric estimation:** ["Adaptive Bayesian density estimation in sup-norm"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.05816); ["Tails assumptions and posterior concentration rates for mixtures of Gaussians"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.06536) (with J. Rousseau); risk of the minimum-norm estimator in spike covariance ([with Y. Mahdaviyeh](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.13421)).

Other recent work: change-point detection in preferential attachment graphs ([with I. Kaddouri and E. Gassiat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18685)), robust community detection ([SubSearch, with L. Bianco and C. Keribin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03657)).
:::

::: note
[Common thread]{.tag} This work shares a signature: **guarantees** (minimaxity, concentration rates, exact risk) for **usable procedures** on real data — exactly the ambition of this module at the M1 level, and its M2 extension (privacy, uncertainty, calibration).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **Randomization by hand.** Data 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, split 3+3. Enumerate the 20 allocations, compute all values of $\hat d$, recover $p = 0.10$ and the exact distribution (stem-and-leaf display). Which split gives exactly $\hat d = 2.33$?
2.  **Power.** (a) Redo the computation of 2.5 for $\delta/\sigma = 0.4$ and 85 % power. (b) A two-sided test has $\alpha = 5\,\%$ and $n = 50$ per group: plot $\pi(\delta)$ for $\delta/\sigma \in [0; 1]$ and read off the smallest detectable effect size with 80 % power. (c) For proportions ($p_A = 0.10$, expected effect +1 point), adapt the formula by replacing $2\sigma^2$ with $p_A(1-p_A) + p_B(1-p_B)$ and compute $n$.
3.  **Simpson.** Verify all the cells of table 3.2 (82.8 %, etc.), then recompute the overall rates by standardizing on A's profile and on B's; comment on the sensitivity to the profile choice.
4.  **DiD.** With table 4.4: compute the naive before/after comparison, the cross-sectional after comparison, and the DiD; check that the DiD equals the interaction coefficient of the model $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{NJ} + \beta_2 \text{After} + \beta_3 (\text{NJ} \times \text{After}) + e$. Simulate 500 restaurants with common AR(1) shocks and show that naive standard errors are 3–5× too small without clustering (Bertrand et al. 2004).
5.  **BH in practice.** (a) Apply Bonferroni, Holm and BH to the p-values of example 6.4 for $q = \alpha = 0.10$ and $q = 0.01$. (b) Simulation: generate $m = 1000$ p-values ($m_0 = 900$ uniform, 100 false nulls with p \~ Beta(1, 8)), repeat 500 times, estimate the empirical FWER and FDR of each procedure and verify the calibration $\mathrm{FDR} \approx q\, m_0/m$.
6.  **Regression.** On the `cars` dataset (or an equivalent): fit $d \sim s$, plot the 4 diagnostics, apply Box-Cox, refit; identify the point with the largest Cook's distance, redo without it; compare the classical and HC1 standard errors (`statsmodels`).
7.  **Peeking.** Simulate 1000 A/B tests under $H_0$ (two Bernoulli $p = 0.10$, $n = 10^5$ per arm): (a) a single look at midpoint — false positive rate; (b) daily looks for 28 days with stopping if p \< 0.05 — compare with the 22.6 % of the union bound and with the bound of Johari et al.; (c) implement a Gaussian mSPRT and verify its "always" validity.
8.  **Bayesian A/B.** Take up the code of ch. 8: (a) analyze the sensitivity to the Beta(1,1) vs Beta(10,10) prior; (b) turn the decision rule into "expected loss \< cost of a rollout"; (c) add the per-segment analysis (mobile/desktop) with BH correction of the interaction tests; (d) relate to the frequentist Wald CI — when do they diverge?
9.  **RCBD.** Add to the data of 9.1 a moderate block × variety (interaction) effect, redo the ANOVA, test the interaction; build the same trial under a completely randomized design (same values, assignment blind to the blocks) and show the loss of F. Write the simultaneous (Tukey) confidence interval for the 6 comparisons.
10. **Communication.** You have $\hat d = 3.1$, 95 % CI = \[−3.5; 9.7\], p = 0.041, $n = 80$. Write in 5 lines: (a) a misleading "press" summary; (b) an honest summary; (c) list the three graphical manipulations that would reverse the reader's impression, and their fixes.
11. **Project.** INRAE or open data from a blocked trial (or kaggle: agricultural crop yield): from plan to conclusions — map the potential biases, justify the plan, ANOVA + diagnostics, bootstrap of the contrasts, multiple-comparison correction, final one-page report with honest visualizations and limits. Grading: 40 % plan, 40 % correct analysis, 20 % communication.
